units.sourceHTML: Trying out the language #
units.originalInnerHTML: Trying out the language #

units.sourceHTML: If you’d like to try Wren, you have a few options.
units.originalInnerHTML: If you’d like to try Wren, you have a few options.

units.sourceHTML: In your browser. You can try Wren right here!
units.originalInnerHTML: In your browser. You can try Wren right here!

units.sourceHTML: On your computer. The Wren CLI project is a downloadable executable to run scripts with access to file io and more. See the Wren CLI docs.
units.originalInnerHTML: On your computer. The Wren CLI project is a downloadable executable to run scripts with access to file io and more. See the Wren CLI docs.

units.sourceHTML:
Embedded in your code. See how to build and embed Wren below.
And then read the embedding guide!
units.originalInnerHTML:
Embedded in your code. See how to build and embed Wren below.
And then read the embedding guide!

units.sourceHTML: Once you have somewhere to explore, it’s time to learn the language.
units.originalInnerHTML: Once you have somewhere to explore, it’s time to learn the language.

units.sourceHTML: Embed the VM #
units.originalInnerHTML: Embed the VM #

units.sourceHTML: The Wren Virtual Machine is the core of the language that executes Wren source code. It is just a library, not a standalone application. It’s designed to be embedded in a larger host application.
units.originalInnerHTML: The Wren Virtual Machine is the core of the language that executes Wren source code. It is just a library, not a standalone application. It’s designed to be embedded in a larger host application.

units.sourceHTML:
It has no dependencies beyond the C standard library.
You can use it as a static library, shared library, or simply compile the source into your app.
units.originalInnerHTML:
It has no dependencies beyond the C standard library.
You can use it as a static library, shared library, or simply compile the source into your app.

units.sourceHTML: Building Wren #
units.originalInnerHTML: Building Wren #

units.sourceHTML:
To build the Wren library, we look inside the ⟦CODE0⟧ folder.
In here you’ll find ready to go projects for ⟦CODE1⟧, ⟦CODE2⟧ and tools like ⟦CODE3⟧.
units.originalInnerHTML: To build the Wren library, we look inside the projects/ folder. In here you’ll find ready to go projects for Visual Studio, XCode and tools like make.

units.sourceHTML: Windows Open ⟦CODE0⟧ inside ⟦CODE1⟧ (or ⟦CODE2⟧), hit build.
units.originalInnerHTML: Windows Open wren.sln inside projects/vs2019/ (or vs2017), hit build.

units.sourceHTML: Mac Open ⟦CODE0⟧ inside ⟦CODE1⟧, hit build.
units.originalInnerHTML: Mac Open wren.xcworkspace inside projects/xcode/, hit build.

units.sourceHTML: Linux Run ⟦CODE0⟧ inside of ⟦CODE1⟧.
units.originalInnerHTML: Linux Run make inside of projects/make/.

units.sourceHTML:
In each case, there will be library files generated into the root ⟦CODE0⟧ folder.
These are what you’ll link into your project, based on your needs.
units.originalInnerHTML:
In each case, there will be library files generated into the root lib/ folder.
These are what you’ll link into your project, based on your needs.

units.sourceHTML: Static Linking ⟦CODE0⟧ on Windows, ⟦CODE1⟧ elsewhere.
units.originalInnerHTML: Static Linking wren.lib on Windows, libwren.a elsewhere.

units.sourceHTML: Dynamic Linking ⟦CODE0⟧ on Windows, ⟦CODE1⟧ on Linux, and ⟦CODE2⟧ on Mac.
units.originalInnerHTML: Dynamic Linking wren.dll on Windows, libwren.so on Linux, and libwren.dylib on Mac.

units.sourceHTML:
Note that the default build will also generate ⟦CODE0⟧ inside of ⟦CODE1⟧,
a binary that is used to run the language tests. It can execute simple scripts.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Note that the default build will also generate wren_test inside of bin/,
a binary that is used to run the language tests. It can execute simple scripts.

units.sourceHTML:
Other platforms
If your platform isn’t explicitly supported, it is recommended that you include the Wren source in your project for a portable experience.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Other platforms
If your platform isn’t explicitly supported, it is recommended that you include the Wren source in your project for a portable experience.

units.sourceHTML: Including the code in your project #
units.originalInnerHTML: Including the code in your project #

units.sourceHTML:
all source files
The alternative to building via the provided projects is to include the wren source code in your project. Since it has no dependencies this is simple, all the code in ⟦CODE0⟧ comes along. There’s a readme in ⟦CODE1⟧ for details.
units.originalInnerHTML:
all source files
The alternative to building via the provided projects is to include the wren source code in your project. Since it has no dependencies this is simple, all the code in src/ comes along. There’s a readme in src/ for details.

units.sourceHTML:
‘amalgamated’ build
If you want an even simpler way, there’s an ‘amalgamated’ build (often called ⟦CODE0⟧, or ⟦CODE1⟧ builds.). This is all of the wren source code in one file.
units.originalInnerHTML:
‘amalgamated’ build
If you want an even simpler way, there’s an ‘amalgamated’ build (often called blob, or unity builds.). This is all of the wren source code in one file.

units.sourceHTML:
This file can be generated by running ⟦CODE0⟧, 
which saves the generated output in ⟦CODE1⟧.
units.originalInnerHTML: This file can be generated by running python3 util/generate_amalgamation.py > build/wren.c, which saves the generated output in build/wren.c.

units.sourceHTML:
Include ⟦CODE0⟧ and ⟦CODE1⟧ in your project code and you’re good to go.
<small>Ideally later we can automate generating this and include it in the repo.</small>
units.originalInnerHTML: Include build/wren.c and src/include/wren.h in your project code and you’re good to go. Ideally later we can automate generating this and include it in the repo.
